ch12.title: The Confession on the Way to Caesarea-Philippi
ch12.b002: Simon Peter could have named the smells of Zebedee’s boatshop with his eyes shut: pitch and wet cedar, nets drying in the sun, curls of wood shaving. It had been ten weeks. On Sunday, August 7, A.D. 29, the Master had come back across the lake to meet his family, and Andrew and Peter had come with him. David Zebedee had arranged it with Jude, the Master’s brother, so that Mary and all the brothers and sisters would be there. It was a meeting that had gone wrong for a long time. Peter stood by the door of the shop and looked up the road again and again.
ch12.b003: But nobody came. A group of Pharisees from Jerusalem, hoping to learn where the Master was, had called at Mary’s house. They read something in the faces of the family and simply settled in on the doorstep. Several times during the day Jude and Ruth tried to slip past the watchers to send word, and every time it was no use. Early in the afternoon David’s messengers brought the news. The Master made no attempt to go to the house. Once again, through no one’s fault, he and his family had failed to meet.
ch12.b004: Peter looked at the Master’s face from the side. He said nothing. Peter found that silence hard to bear. He thought of his own home. Not far from here were his wife and his three children, and he could not go to see them today. But the Master could not go to see his mother. It was the same situation, and yet Peter felt the Master’s disappointment more sharply than his own, all the more because the Master was not a man to let such things show in his face.
ch12.b005: Just then a collector of the temple tax came along. He recognized the Master, drew Peter aside and asked whether their Master did not pay the temple tax. For a moment Peter’s blood rose. The man was asking them to give money to the religion of the very men who had sworn to kill his Master. But he noticed an odd expression on the collector’s face. It was a trap. The man wanted to carry away one sentence refusing the half shekel. Peter swallowed his anger and answered: of course the Master pays the tax. Wait by the gate, and I will bring it to you shortly.
ch12.b006: Only after the words were out did he catch himself. Judas Iscariot carried their money, and Judas was across the lake. Neither Andrew nor the Master had brought any money either. And with the Pharisees looking for them, they could hardly go to Bethsaida to get some. Peter went to the Master and told him plainly. The Master looked at him. If he had promised, he said, then he should pay. But how did he mean to keep his word? Would he turn fisherman again to do it? Still, in the circumstances it was right to pay; they should give these men no reason to take offense. Let Peter take the boat, cast for fish, sell the catch at the market over there, and pay the tax for all three of them.
ch12.b007: As Peter turned toward the boat, the Master added, half in jest, that it was a strange thing for the sons of the king to be paying tribute, since it was usually the stranger who was taxed; but they ought not to put a stumbling block in the way of the authorities. Off with you, he said; perhaps you will catch the fish with the shekel in its mouth.
ch12.b008: Peter burst out laughing. It was the first time he had laughed all day. He climbed into the little boat tied up in front of the shop. When he took hold of the oars his palms remembered the weight before he did. It had been more than two months. But before he could even spread the net, two men came toward him carrying several large baskets of fish. One was a secret messenger of David’s who had been standing nearby and had overheard everything; the other was a fisherman friend whom the messenger had signaled to come in from the shore. They helped Peter carry the baskets to a fish merchant close by. The merchant paid for the catch, the messenger added a little to it, and there was enough for the tax of all three. The collector took the money and let the penalty for late payment go, since they had been away from Galilee for some time.
ch12.b009: Peter laughed to himself as he walked back from paying. There had been no fish with a shekel in its mouth. There had been two men with baskets instead. He liked that better. Better than a coin dropping out of heaven was the fact that there were people quietly following them about to keep watch over the Master. Later the story would be told differently, but what Peter remembered of that day was the reek of fish and the jingling hand of the fish merchant.
ch12.b010: They waited by the shore until nearly sundown. The messengers reported that Mary’s house was still being watched. When it grew dark the three of them got into the boat and rowed slowly toward the eastern shore. Peter looked back as he pulled. Among the lights along that shore was the house of the Master’s mother, and somewhere among them was his own. Andrew rowed opposite him. His brother said nothing at all, but he matched the stroke of his oar to Peter’s.
ch12.b012: On Monday, August 8, more than a hundred people gathered at Magadan Park, near Bethsaida-Julias. Believers, the evangelists, the women’s evangelistic corps and others who cared about the future of the kingdom came over from Capernaum for a conference. Hearing that the Master was there, many Pharisees came too. By now some of the Sadducees had joined them.
ch12.b013: Before the closed meeting with the believers, the Master held a public meeting. The Pharisees heckled and did their best to break it up. Then the leader of the disturbers stepped forward and asked for a sign of his authority to teach, so that when it came to pass, everyone would know that God had sent him.
ch12.b014: Simon Zelotes clenched his fists. He hated the demand, and yet some corner of his heart wanted the Master to grant it. Just once. If only heaven would show something in front of those arrogant faces. Then the scattered crowds would come back, and the days of being hunted would be over. In his years among the Zealots he had sharpened his sword dreaming of such a day. There was no sword in his hand now, but the dream was still there.
ch12.b015: The Master spoke to them about the weather. In the evening, he said, they saw a red sky and said tomorrow would be fair; in the morning they saw the sky red and lowering and said there would be a storm. When a cloud rose in the west they said a shower was coming, and when the south wind blew they said there would be heat. They could read the face of the sky so well; why could they not read the signs of the times? A sign had already been given to those who wanted to know the truth. But to an evil-minded and hypocritical generation, no sign would be given. And with that he withdrew.
ch12.b016: Simon chewed on those words for a long time. A sign had already been given. What sign? He thought back over the last six weeks. The Syrian woman in Sidon, the word dog he himself had thrown at her, and the face that had caught it and turned it aside with a laugh. That day a gentile woman had believed and he had been ashamed. Had that been a sign too? Simon shook his head. A nation was not built on things like that.
ch12.b017: That evening, at the conference with the believers, it was decided that as soon as the Master and the twelve returned from Caesarea-Philippi they would all undertake a united mission through every city and village of the Decapolis. The Master took part in the planning. And as he dismissed them, he warned them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the Sadducees. They should not be taken in by a show of learning or by loyalty to religious forms, he said, but should care only for the spirit of living truth. And when love for their neighbors welled up in their hearts, they should not stifle it but express it in wise service to their neighbors’ real needs.
ch12.b018: As he listened, John Zebedee happened to glance at Judas Iscariot’s face. Judas’s lips were pressed tight together. John did not know what that look meant. He only noticed, that day for the first time, that whenever the word Pharisee was spoken, Judas’s eyes narrowed very slightly. Of the twelve, Judas alone came from Judea. He was taking the warning as a veiled reference to himself. That much John did not see.
ch12.b020: Early on Tuesday morning the Master and the twelve left Magadan Park for Caesarea-Philippi. As they were passing south of the Waters of Merom, the apostles began to tell one another about what had happened to them in Phoenicia and elsewhere: how their message had been received, how the different peoples regarded their Master. Peter talked the most. The twins told about the bridge at Sidon, and Nathaniel imitated some comical Greek he had heard on the docks at Tyre. Philip said the gentiles ate better than he had expected. Everyone laughed.
ch12.b021: At noon they stopped under some mulberry trees beside the road. The broad leaves made a deep shade, and the sunlight trembled through them like scattered coins. When the bread had been shared, the Master suddenly asked them who men said that he was.
ch12.b022: Peter stopped with the bread in his hand. It was the first time the Master had ever asked them a question about himself. For months he had taught them over and over what the kingdom of heaven was. But never once had he asked who he was. More than half the apostles answered. Everyone who knew him, they said, took him for a prophet or an extraordinary man. Even his enemies feared him so much that they explained his power by saying he was in league with the prince of devils. Some in Judea and Samaria who had never met him believed he was John the Baptist risen from the dead. Peter explained that at different times and by different people he had been compared with Moses, Elijah, Isaiah and Jeremiah.
ch12.b023: When the Master had heard all this, he rose to his feet. The twelve were sitting around him in a half circle. He looked down at them. Then, with a wide sweep of his hand that took them all in, he asked with startling force:
ch12.b024: “But who do you say that I am?”
ch12.b025: Nobody answered. The wind turned the mulberry leaves over. The twelve could not take their eyes from him. Peter could hear his own heart. This question was not like the other. To say what men thought, you only had to repeat what others said. But this asked what he himself was staking his life on. He knew the answer. He had known it for a long time: since the wedding at Cana, since the evening the five thousand ate. But once he said it aloud, it could never be taken back.
ch12.b026: He was on his feet before he had thought. It was always that way with him; his words ran ahead of his thinking. But this time it was not his words that ran ahead. It was his whole body.
ch12.b027: “⟦Q 157:3.5⟧You are the Deliverer, the Son of the living God.⟦/Q⟧”
ch12.b028: His voice cracked. In that same instant the eleven who were sitting rose together to their feet. Peter did not turn around, but he felt it: the brush of robes, the small sound of a piece of bread falling from someone’s lap. He was not alone. He had spoken for all of them.
ch12.b029: John was standing right behind Peter. He looked at Peter’s back, the broad, sweat-soaked back of a fisherman, and saw that it was trembling. John realized that he had wanted to be the one to say it. He had been among the very first to know this man. He had long looked after the Master’s family affairs and knew how dearly the Master cared for his mother. Yet the words had come from Peter’s mouth. Jealousy rose as far as his throat, and then, strangely, sank away again. It did not matter whose mouth the words had come from. All twelve were standing. John was glad simply to be one of those who stood.
ch12.b030: Simon Zelotes stood with his jaw clenched. Deliverer: that was what Peter had said. To Simon that word meant, before anything else, the one who would free Israel from the yoke of the gentiles. And the Son of God. Then the deliverance was guaranteed by heaven itself. Simon’s heart pounded. He remembered himself the day before at Magadan, hungry for a sign. What need was there of a sign? The Son of God was standing right here.
ch12.b031: The Master motioned them to sit down. Still standing, he told them that this had been revealed to them by his Father. The hour had come for them to know the truth about him. But for the present they must tell no one. And now, he said, let us go on from here.
ch12.b033: They took to the road again and reached Caesarea-Philippi late that evening. It was a valley where the Jordan poured out of a cave in the earth, with the heights of Hermon in full view to the north. A man named Celsus was expecting them. They settled into his house, but the apostles hardly slept that night. Each of them sensed that something great had happened in their lives and in the work of the kingdom.
ch12.b034: The two Simons talked with their brethren all night long. Peter and Simon Zelotes were almost of one mind about the Master. They wanted every one of the others to accept him with their whole hearts, not merely as the Messiah but as the divine Son of the living God. So they took the others one at a time, by the lamp, in the courtyard, at the well.
ch12.b035: Simon Zelotes was good at this. Settling a wavering man’s mind in about fifteen minutes was his gift. He went to Thomas. Thomas did not accept the matter easily. How could a man be the Son of God, he asked; first tell me what the words even mean. Simon drew a breath. What they meant. He could not explain all of that. He could only tell what he had seen: a man who did not lose his temper, who could bend men without a sword, who was calmer while he was hunted than the men hunting him. That calm, Simon said, did not come from any man. Thomas listened for a long time and then nodded. He did not look persuaded so much as like a man who had found the same thing confirmed in other words.
ch12.b036: But as he talked, Simon surprised himself a little. He was talking about the Master’s calmness. He was not talking about the sword. It was the first time a Zealot had explained the Messiah without mentioning the sword. He held that fact for a moment and then put it down. Since he was the Son of God, Simon decided, when the time came he would win without any need of swords. That settled it for him. Whether it was really the same deliverance he had always dreamed of, he did not ask.
ch12.b037: Peter talked the whole night: to the twins, to Philip, to Matthew. Then, toward dawn, when he found himself alone in a corner of the courtyard, he was suddenly afraid. Had it really been he who said those words at noon? He knew himself. He was a man who made a resolution in the morning and broke it by evening. And from the mouth of such a man those words had come. He looked down at his hands. Yesterday those hands had gripped an oar and hauled baskets of fish. Today they had pointed to the Son of God. The distance between the two made him dizzy.
ch12.b038: Andrew came over and sat down beside him. His brother asked nothing. Then, after a long while, he said only this:
ch12.b040: Peter looked at him. Andrew was already looking at the sky. It was not praise. Andrew did not know how to give praise. But Peter knew it was the closest thing to praise his brother could say. From about this time, although Andrew remained the director of the apostolic corps, the voice of the twelve more and more became Peter’s. It happened by common consent. And Andrew was the first to consent.
ch12.b042: Late on Wednesday morning the apostles gathered in Celsus’s garden for the noon meal. Their faces were grave and solemn. The night’s talk still sat upon them. About noon the Master came into the garden, and they all rose to their feet, like courtiers before a king.
ch12.b043: The Master looked at them and smiled. It was that friendly, brotherly smile of his, the one he wore whenever his followers took themselves, or something that concerned them, too seriously. In an instant the tension in the garden melted. He motioned them to sit down. Never again did the twelve rise to greet him when he came among them. They had seen that he did not welcome such outward shows of respect.
ch12.b044: John remembered that smile for a long time. They had stayed up all night talking about the Son of God. And then in the morning the Son of God walked into the garden, saw their stiff faces and smiled. A man who carried the weight of heaven did not use that weight to press anyone down. John felt that it told him more than anything they had said in the night.
ch12.b045: When they had eaten and were talking over plans for the Decapolis tour, the Master suddenly looked up into their faces. A full day had passed, he said, since they had agreed with Peter’s declaration about who he was. Did they still hold to their decision? The twelve stood up. This time they did not stand to greet him; they stood to answer. Peter stepped a few paces forward. Yes, he said, they did. They believed that he was the Son of the living God. And he sat down again among his brothers.
ch12.b046: The Master, still standing, spoke to them. They were his chosen ambassadors, he said, but they could never have come to this belief through human knowledge alone. It was a revelation of his Father’s spirit to their inmost souls. And since they made this confession by the insight of the Father’s spirit dwelling within them, upon this foundation he would build the brotherhood of the kingdom of heaven. On this rock of spiritual reality he would build a living temple of spiritual fellowship in the eternal realities of the Father’s kingdom. No forces of evil would prevail against it.
ch12.b047: Peter shivered at the word rock. It was what his name meant, the nickname the Master had given him long ago with a smile. But the Master was not pointing at him now. He was pointing at the confession itself, at the truth the spirit had shown them. Peter did not fully grasp the difference that day. He only knew that something was to be built on words that had come out of the mouth of a man like him, and that it frightened him and made him grateful at once.
ch12.b048: The Master went on. The Father’s spirit, he said, would be the guide and teacher of all who entered this fellowship, but to them and to those who came after them he was now handing over the keys of the outward kingdom: authority over temporal things, the social and economic side of this association of men and women. And once more he charged them to tell no one, for the present, that he was the Son of God.
ch12.b049: Simon Zelotes lifted his head at the word keys. The keys of the kingdom. He heard it as the sound of a door swinging open: the keys of a city gate, the keys of a palace. The part about the keys being authority over the outward affairs of the kingdom, over the practical life of the fellowship, slipped past him. What he heard was only that the keys had been given to them. The Simon of that day had no idea what shame that misunderstanding would bring him a few days later on the slopes of Hermon.
ch12.b050: On that day the Master began to believe in the faith of his apostles. A faith that had come through the trials they had just passed through, he judged, would also come through the fiery trials ahead, and would emerge from the apparent wreck of all their hopes into a new light. But there was one among the twelve of whom this was not true.
ch12.b052: When he had finished, the Master told the twelve to go apart into the hills until the evening meal and seek wisdom, strength and spiritual guidance. They did as he said. On the hill behind Celsus’s house the twelve scattered and sat down alone.
ch12.b053: Simon Zelotes knelt on a rock near the top of the hill. He was a man who had had to learn prayer all over again from the Master. In his Zealot days his prayers had been oaths: let me drive out the gentiles, let me wash the land in the blood of our enemies. Today he said nothing like that. He only gave thanks that he had been allowed to stand beside the Son of God, and asked to live to see the day that Son would raise Israel up. The word sword had dropped out of his prayer. But the word Israel had not. He did not yet understand how the two were different. Still, when he got up, his heart was light. At least his prayer had not made room for fear.
ch12.b054: Judas Iscariot went up into the hills too. He sat down in the shadow of a rock and closed his eyes. But his thoughts did not go toward prayer. They went where they always went. The day John the Baptist was beheaded. The times he had been rebuked by the Master. The day the crowd wanted to make the Master king and he drew back. The morning they fled from the Pharisees. Yesterday, when he refused their challenge to give a sign. And the empty money bag. If he was the Son of God, why did he not use his power? Why did he always draw back? Yesterday’s words about leaven had lodged in him like a thorn. Every time the Master sent the apostles away to pray alone, Judas sat like this, and instead of communing with the spiritual world, he sank into human fears. He nursed subtle doubts and gave room to the wish to repay his hurts. That was his great mistake. And that day was no different.
ch12.b055: When they came back to the garden in the evening, the Master told them many new things. Some of them sounded strange even to their ears. From now on, he said, anyone who wanted fellowship with them must take on the obligations of sonship and follow him. And when he was no longer with them, they should not imagine that the world would treat them better than it had treated their Master. The Son of Man had come to serve, and to give his life as a gift for all. He had come forth from the Father into this world; before Abraham was, he was. And soon he must leave this world and go back to his Father’s work.
ch12.b056: James Zebedee did not once raise his eyes while the Master spoke. He was a man who looked at everything from every side. Before Abraham, and soon to leave: the same mouth had said both. He tried to hold the two together.
ch12.b057: John caught his breath at the words. Soon to leave. He had heard that before. On the highland the day they knelt to be ordained, the Master had spoken of the time when he would presently leave them, and only Andrew and John had caught it. Since then John had kept those words folded away in a corner of his heart. Today they unfolded again, and this time they were plainer. He looked at his brother James. James said nothing. Today that silence frightened him.
ch12.b058: The Master went on. His kingdom was not of this world. Foxes had holes and birds had nests, but he had nowhere to lay his head; could they believe in him even so? And yet the Father and he were one, he told them, and whoever had seen him had seen the Father. The Father would never leave him alone, and he would never forsake them when they went out to carry the gospel to the world. He had brought them apart like this so that they might understand the glory and grandeur of the life to which he had called them.
ch12.b059: The apostles heard those bold and startling words in silence. Nobody asked anything, not even Peter. They were stunned. Then they broke up into small groups to talk the words over and argue about them. The twins looked at each other and tilted their heads. Matthew sat by the lamp writing down what he had heard before he forgot it. Nathaniel and Thomas talked in low voices for a long time at the far end of the garden. They had confessed him to be the Son of God. But they could not yet grasp the full meaning of what they had been led to confess.
ch12.b061: That evening Andrew took it upon himself to talk with each of his brothers in turn: with Peter, with James and John, with Philip and Nathaniel, with Matthew and Thomas, with the twins and Simon Zelotes. They were searching talks, and each man came away strengthened. But there was one with whom it did not happen. That was Judas Iscariot.
ch12.b062: Andrew had never been as close to Judas as to the other apostles. Judas had never once opened his heart freely to the head of the apostolic corps. For a long time Andrew had not thought this serious. Hearts opened at different speeds, he told himself. But tonight he felt differently. Judas’s attitude worried him too much. The hand that had torn at blades of grass on the ordination highland; the face half lit by the fire. Things he had filed away came back to him all at once.
ch12.b063: Late that night, when everyone was fast asleep, Andrew went to find the Master. John happened to be awake. He saw Andrew cross the dark courtyard quietly toward the room where the Master was staying. He could not tell what it was about. It was rare for the chief to go to the Master in the middle of the night. John closed his eyes again, but sleep was slow in coming.
ch12.b064: Andrew laid his worry before the Master. The Master told him it was not wrong for him to come about this, but there was nothing more that they could do. Only, he said, go on placing the greatest confidence in this apostle. And say nothing to the others about this talk.
ch12.b065: That was all Andrew could draw from him. He came out of the room and stood in the dark courtyard. Nothing more that we can do. The words pressed on his chest. He was the chief. Watching to see who was tired, who was wavering, and doing something about it was his work. But this time there was nothing he could do. All that was left was to go on trusting, and to keep silent. That night, for the first time, Andrew learned how heavy those two things were. He looked once toward the place where Judas lay, then went back to his own place and lay down. Sleep did not come.
ch12.b066: The other apostles had gone through the same disappointments and trials. The death of John the Baptist, the days of being hunted, the empty treasury: they had all borne them together. But they loved Jesus. At least they must have loved him more than Judas did, because they went with him to the bitter end.
ch12.b067: The Money Bag and the Mountain
ch12.b068: On Thursday they stayed one more day at Celsus’s house, waiting for money that David Zebedee was to send. Since the crowds had melted away in Galilee, their income had fallen off badly, and when they reached Caesarea-Philippi the treasury was empty. In the morning Judas turned the empty bag inside out and gave a sour smile.
ch12.b069: Matthew Levi’s heart ached when he saw that smile. At times like this he had always opened his own purse, under other names, without anyone knowing. But this time there was no purse to open. He had no ready money in hand. Nor could he leave the Master and his brothers to go and raise funds; at a time like this, leaving was the last thing he wanted to do. All he could do was arrange for the sale of his last piece of property in Capernaum, with instructions that the money be turned over to Judas anonymously when it came. That would be the end of it. After that there would be nothing left for him either.
ch12.b070: That evening David’s messengers arrived from Bethsaida. David had foreseen such a day, and he had told his messengers to collect money for the exiled Master and apostles as they passed through Judea, Samaria and Galilee. What they brought was enough to keep them until they began the Decapolis tour. Judas counted the money and put it into the bag. His face eased a little. Matthew breathed again too. Nobody looked at Matthew. That was what he had wanted, and it was also the loneliest thing of all.
ch12.b071: On the morning of Friday, August 12, the Master spoke to the twelve. Lay in provisions, he told them, and get ready for a journey to the mountain over there. The spirit was bidding him go there to be endowed for the finishing of his work on earth. And he would take his brothers with him, so that they too might be strengthened by sharing the experience, for the trying times ahead.
ch12.b072: Peter looked up to the north. The summit of Hermon shone white in the morning sun. Three days ago under the mulberry trees he had said it: the Son of the living God. The words still seemed to linger in his mouth. He shouldered his sack and stood up. He did not know what was waiting for them. But he no longer asked. He had said those words about this man, and now he had only to follow him.
ch12.b074: The events follow Paper 157, “At Caesarea-Philippi”: the meeting with the family prevented by the Pharisees’ watch (157:0.1–0.2); the temple-tax collector and Peter’s promise, Jesus’ half-humorous remark, the fish brought by David’s messenger and the fisherman friend, the waived penalty, and the return to the eastern shore after dark (157:1.1–1.5); the public meeting at Magadan, the demand for a sign, the answer about the face of the sky, the decision on the Decapolis mission and the warning about leaven (157:2.1–2.2); the talk south of the Waters of Merom, the question under the mulberry trees, Peter’s confession, the eleven rising, and the sleepless night at the home of Celsus (157:3.1–3.7); the work of the two Simons and Peter’s growing role as spokesman, the rising in the garden and Jesus’ smile, the second confession, the words about the rock and the keys, the Master’s new faith in the apostles save one, and the hours of prayer in the hills (157:4.1–4.8); the new teachings in the garden and the apostles’ silence (157:6.7–6.15); Andrew’s talks, his worry over Judas and Jesus’ reply, Judas’s disappointments and his error in the times of prayer (157:7.1–7.4); the day of waiting for funds, Matthew’s last property, David’s messengers, and the instruction of August 12 (157:6.1, 7.5).
ch12.b075: Character facts come from Paper 139: Peter’s family and temperament (139:2.1), John’s charge of Jesus’ family affairs (139:4.1), James’s silences and his ability to see all sides (139:3.3–3.4), Simon Zelotes’s gift for persuasion, his admiration of the Master’s calmness and his material-mindedness (139:11.3–11.5), Matthew’s secret giving (139:7.8–7.9), and Andrew’s reticence in praise and his early sense of trouble in Judas (139:1.8, 1.10).
ch12.b076: Fictional additions are small: the inner thoughts and memories of Peter, John and Simon Zelotes; the boatshop, the mulberry shade and the house of Celsus; what each man talked about south of Merom; Simon persuading Thomas; Andrew’s words to Peter in the courtyard at dawn; John noticing Judas’s face and seeing Andrew go to the Master by night; what each man did in the garden afterward; and Judas turning out the empty bag. One short question of Jesus is given as spoken dialogue.
ch12.b077: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
